## This week's contents
We focus on **restricted maximum likelihood**, which involves estimating the linear regression model under single or multiple linear restrictions. This topic is not completely new, as we considered restricted least squares before. Moreover, we consider three well-known tests for multiple restrictions in the framework of maximum likelihood. These are the **Wald test** (which uses the unrestricted estimates), the **Lagrange Multiplier test** (which uses the restricted estimates) and the **Likelihood Ratio test** (which uses both estimates). In practice, the tests can also be used to decide between an unrestricted and restricted model.

We finish this week by revisiting the concept of **sampling distribution**. To study the behavior of an estimator or test statistic, we require a large number of samples from the same data generation process. We can use **Monte Carlo simulation studies** for this. This way, we can investigate what happens under **correct specification** and **misspecification**.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}

## Sampling distribution
During this course, we discussed at various occassions that many of our statistical quantities of interest are functions of the data. Because of this, they take different values from the one sample to the other. So far, we mainly focused on our estimators but the argument can be extended to e.g. test statistics, predictions and measures of fit. If we had many samples originating from the sample data-generation process at our disposal, then we could obtain its sampling distribution.

Let us focus once more on estimators. We have studied least squares and maximum likelihood, and over the past weeks we have established some properties of these estimators. In particular, we found that under Assumptions (2.1)-(2.4), the least-squares estimator of $\beta$ in the linear regression model $y = X\beta + u$ is the best linear unbiased estimator. The maximum likelihood estimator of $\beta$ exactly coincides with the least-squares estimator, so they share the same properties. However, we have seen that the estimator for the error variance differs. In the least-squares framework, we derived $s^{2} = e'e/(n-k)$ as a natural estimator of $\sigma^{2}$ because it is an unbiased estimator which is best in the class of quadratic estimators under normality. However, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\sigma^{2}$ is given by $\hat{\sigma}^{2} = e'e/n$, which is clearly not unbiased. However, it does have the property of invariance. A particular case in which this is useful, is when we consider $\sigma$, the standard deviation of the error term. Since $\hat{\sigma}^{2} = e'e/n$ is the maximum likelihood estimator of $\sigma^{2}$, we know that $\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^{2}}$ is the maximum likelihood estimator for $\sigma$, provided $\sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^{2}}$ is defined. A similar claim cannot be made for $s = \sqrt{s^{2}}$, which could be a natural candidate to estimate $\sigma$ based on least squares. 

::: {.callout-note title="The standard deviation of the error term" collapse = "true"}

Suppose we consider $s = \sqrt{e'e/(n-k)}$, which is also known as the standard error of the regression (SER), as an estimator for the population standard deviation of the error term. Because $s^{2}$ is unbiased for $\sigma^{2}$, it could be a good candidate to consider.

However, the induced transformation is $g(t) = \sqrt{t}$ is strictly concave for all $t > 0$ because its second derivative is strictly negative. (You may verify $g'(t) = 1/2\sqrt{t}$ and $g''(t) = -1/4t^{3/2}$). Using Jensen's inequality, we know that
$$
E(\sqrt{s^{2}}) < \sqrt{E(s^{2})},
$$
as $g(t) = \sqrt{t}$ is strictly concave. Simplifying both sides of the inequality yields
$$
E(s) < \sigma,
$$
which can be interpreted as the estimator $s$ systematically underestimating the true standard deviation $\sigma$.

:::

Why did we discuss all of the above? They are merely examples of properties that we have established theoretically but cannot easily be understood empirically. As we have seen, unbiasedness of an estimator is a useful property but less so whenever the variance is substantially large. However, in practice, we only observe one sample (or at the very best a few) and it is not viable to make clear statements on the sampling distribution of an estimator. For this reason, we consider Monte Carlo simulation studies next. 

## Monte Carlo simulation study
A power tool in econometrics is the use of **Monte Carlo simulation studies**. The name comes from the famous Monte Carlo Casino in Monaco, in which many of the games such as roulette, dice games and slot machines rely fundamentally on randomness and chance.

The idea behind Monte Carlo simulation studies is quite intuitive. If we can generate many sample from a data-generation process of our choice, then we can evaluate our quantity of interest on all those different samples and learn about its properties. In a sense you could say that researchers plays a schizophrenic role: first they know the truth, then they do not. That is, they first determine exactly how the data is generated by choosing parameter values and the distribution of the different variables. Afterwards, they perform typical operations of interest on the data such as estimation, prediction, testing and save the outcome. They repeat the process many times and obtain the sampling distribution of their object of interest.

::: {.callout-note title="A simple simulation study" collapse = "true"}

Suppose we want to investigate the performance of the least-squares estimator of $\beta_{2}$ in the simple linear regression model.

We generate data according to some rule 
$$
y_{i} = 5 + 2 x_{i} + u_{i},
$$ {#eq-simstudy}
such that the true parameter values are $\beta_{1} = 5$ and $\beta_{2} = 2$. You assume $x_{i} \sim N(50, 3)$ and $u_{i} \sim N(0,1)$, both independent and identially distributed (other choices could be made here).

If the data is generated in this way, we know that it adheres to the Assumptions (2.1) - (2.4). Thus, we expect our estimator $\hat{\beta}_{2}$ to be unbiased (for any sample size $n$) and its variance to decrease as sample size $n$ grows larger.

We can investigate this using a Monte Carlo simulation study as follows:

1. Generate the data according to (@eq-simstudy).
2. Estimate $y_{i} = \beta_{1} + \beta_{2} x_{i} + u_{i}$ by least squares and save the corresponding $\hat{\beta}_{2}$.
3. Repeat Steps 1 and 2 a large amount of time, say $M = 10,000$ times. We call those $M$ *iterations*.
4. You now have a vector with $M$ different estimates of $\hat{\beta}_{2}$. You can study its properties by plotting it (e.g. in a histogram) and compute its average over all iterations. This average should be equal to the true value $\beta_{2}$ in case the estimator is unbiased.

Note that we kept it simple in this example. To investigate whether the variance decreases (and at what rate) when sample size increases, you would perform the same simulation study multiple times where you vary $n$ (for example, you take $n \in \{50, 100, 250, 500, 1000\}$). Moreover, you may save other objects of interest and evaluate them differently. 

:::
 
Based on the example, we can make some claims. Firstly, a simulation study requires the researcher to set up a proper research design which depends on the research question at hand. For example, if you want to investigate unbiasedness you may want to evaluate *the average* of all estimated $\beta$ values. However, if you want to investigate the effect of a Type-I error, you might want to perform a test in every iteration and *count how often you falsely reject* the null hypothesis. If your Type I error (also known as the significance level) is set to $\alpha = 0.05$, you expect in about $0.05 \times 10,000 = 500$ iterations to falsely reject the null hypothesis. Secondly, you may want to investigate how a statistical quantity performs whenever one of the assumptions is not met. For example, you can investigate whether $\hat{\beta}$ is still unbiased whenever the error term is not normally distributed. Or alternatively, you could investigate what happens with the estimator whenever $\Var(u) = \Omega \neq \sigma^{2}I_{n}$ (and compare both scenarios). 

Such scenarios could be challenging to study theoretically, while Monte Carlo simulation studies are easily executed. The main disadvantage is that they are rather case-specific, as you have to define a particular data-generation process in the first step. However, that is why researchers typically consider a large variety of scenarios. Also keep in mind that the theory in this course is well-developed and well-studied. However, in state-of-the-art research (as you will do for your bachelor thesis), the theory is often not (completely) known. You may expect your estimator to have certain properties, but you do not know certainly. In that case, it might help to run some different simulation studies first, as it is typically more costly to write out difficult proofs than running Monte Carlo simulations. If the simulations based on a well-defined data-generation process hint at a biased estimator, you probably do not want to waste your time proving unbiasedness theoretically.
